title: The Photocopy Chain: The Mammal Brain-Mass Canon Disagrees With Itself on 30% of Shared Species, and Three-Quarters of Its Most-Cited Values Cannot Be Traced to a Measurement
description: Comparative neuroscience treats three compilations — Burger et al. (2019), Smaers et al. (2021) and Tsuboi et al. (2018) — as the primary record of mammal brain mass. We pre-registered two tests of that record before downloading any data. Test A diffed the three canons against each other: of the 1,467 species present in at least two canons, 447 (30.47%) disagree by more than 5% on brain mass, and 19.3% disagree by more than 10% — against a registered kill threshold of 3%. Test B traced a pre-registered random sample of 60 Burger values to their sources: only 15 (25.0%) terminate in a work whose authors themselves measured brains or endocranial volumes; the remaining 75% terminate in earlier compilations — against a registered kill threshold of 85% traceable. Both legs fail their kill conditions decisively. Burger's 1,552 values cite only 30 distinct first sources, and five compilations supply 82.6% of them. The canon's worst errors — an owl monkey at 6.7× its measured brain mass, a laboratory rat at 3.4× — are traceable, but to mislabelled or unreplicated specimen records from 1908 and 1940 that no later compiler re-checked. No canon is the accurate one: each dissents from the other two, and one carries a clade-shaped divergence across the pinnipeds. The mammal brain-mass canon is a photocopy chain, and any analysis built on a single canon inherits whichever copy it happened to open. Keywords: brain mass; comparative neuroanatomy; data provenance; Burger et al. 2019; Smaers et al. 2021; Tsuboi et al. 2018; pre-registration; measurement
